default.p.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-p1.vietnamese:
When listening to someone speak, Japanese people often use many verbal backchannels. Aizuchi means repeatedly saying things such as “uh-huh,” “I see,” and “that’s right,” or nodding up and down. Backchannels convey messages such as, “I am listening to your story,” and “Please go on.”

However, in other countries, some cultures believe that when listening to someone, one should look the other person in the eyes and say nothing until they have finished speaking. Suppose that person and a Japanese person have a conversation. The foreign speaker may find it noisy or annoying because the Japanese listener keeps responding with expressions such as “uh-huh” and “yes, yes.” Conversely, when the Japanese person is speaking, the absence of backchannels from the foreign listener may make the Japanese speaker feel uneasy.

When cultures differ, communication styles differ as well. Therefore, Japanese people and people from other countries should understand that the way they convey “I am listening to your story” is different, and should think about how to communicate. If they do so, they will surely be able to communicate comfortably and pleasantly, whether or not they use backchannels.

A

default.p.goukakumoshi3_n4-t8-p1.vietnamese:
A Trip to Kyoto

Alberto

I went to Kyoto last week. Kyoto has many historic Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples. The temple I found most interesting was Kinkaku-ji. Kinkaku-ji was built in 1394 by a man named Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. Kinkaku-ji is gold-colored and very beautiful. I also thought the temple's garden was beautiful.

I took many pictures of Kinkaku-ji. At that time, a Japanese student asked me, "Excuse me, could you take a picture for me?" I replied, "Of course," and took a picture for the student. Afterward, I had a long conversation in Japanese with the student. I had a wonderful time.

I have come to like Kyoto very much. I would like to visit Kyoto again someday.

default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t10-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) ごはんなどを食べながら、お酒を飲む。
The passage warns that drinking only alcohol without eating anything is bad for the body. Therefore, drinking alcohol while eating rice or other food is the appropriate choice.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t10-q1.explanation: The pattern 「〜ながら」 means “while doing〜” or “doing〜 at the same time as〜”; here, it means eating food while drinking alcohol. The sentence 「何も食べないで、お酒だけを飲む飲み方も、体にはよくないので、注意してください」 means “Please also be careful, because drinking only alcohol without eating anything is bad for the body.” The supporting sentence from the passage is: 「また、何も食べないで、お酒だけを飲む飲み方も、体にはよくないので、注意してください。」. A useful tip is that (c) and (d) are directly rejected by 「やめましょう」, while (a) is the opposite of drinking 「お酒だけ」.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t11-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 大きい部屋を新しく予約する。
Yamakawa needs to arrange a change to a larger meeting room because the current room is too small. Therefore, he needs to reserve a new large room.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t11-q1.explanation: The pattern 「～ので、～てもらえますか」 gives a reason and makes a polite request, meaning “Because…, could you please…?”. The sentence means: “Because the room for today’s meeting is too small, could you change it to a slightly larger room?”. The supporting sentence is: 「今日、会議をする部屋はせますぎるので、もう少し大きい部屋に変えてもらえますか。」. A useful tip is that the computer and the materials have already been assigned to other people, while changing to a larger room is the task requested of Yamakawa.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t12-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 子どもたちに動物の絵や写真をあげる。
The passage says that this person shows children pictures and photographs of animals while explaining things clearly; it does not say that the person gives the pictures or photographs to them.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t12-q1.explanation: The pattern ～たり、～たりする lists representative actions; here, the work includes guiding customers and explaining animals. The relevant sentence means: “So that children can understand various things about animals, I try to speak clearly while showing them pictures and photographs of animals.” The exact supporting sentence is: 「子どもたちには、動物のことがいろいろわかるように、動物の絵や写真を見せながら、わかりやすく話すようにしています。」The key distinction is between 見せる, “to show,” and あげる, “to give”: the passage only says that the pictures and photographs are shown, so (c) is not part of the job.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 日本人は、だれかが話しているときに、たくさんあいづちを打つから。
The passage says that Japanese people use many backchannel responses while listening, so some foreigners may find this noisy.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-q1.explanation: The pattern 「～と思う人もいる」 means “some people may think that～,” while 「～ので」 expresses a reason or cause. The question asks why some people find the behavior noisy, and the relevant main idea is that Japanese listeners repeatedly use many あいづち while someone is speaking. The supporting sentence is: 「もし、その人と日本人が話すことがあったら、話している外国人には、話を聞いている日本人が「うん、うん」、「はい、はい」などのことばを言い続けるので、うるさいと思う人もいるだろう。」, meaning that a foreign speaker may think the Japanese listener is noisy because the listener keeps saying expressions such as “uh-huh” and “yes, yes.” Option (d) is the easiest to confuse with the correct answer because it mentions 「うん、うん」 and 「はい、はい」, but the passage says Japanese people use various あいづち and nod their heads, not only those two expressions.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 相手が、話を聞いていないのではないかと思うから。
Japanese speakers feel anxious because foreigners do not respond with あいづち, so they worry that the other person may not be listening.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-q2.explanation: The pattern 「〜のではないかと思う」 means “think that perhaps…” and expresses a supposition; 「〜てしまう」 in 「不安に思ってしまう」 adds the nuance of an unintended or unavoidable feeling of anxiety. The sentence means: “Conversely, when Japanese people are speaking, they often feel anxious because foreigners do not respond with あいづち.” The textual evidence is: 「反対に、日本人は話をしているとき、外国人があいづちを打たないので、②不安に思ってしまうことが多いのではないかと思う。」To distinguish it from (d), remember that 「うるさいと思う」 is the foreigner’s possible reaction to Japanese あいづち, while 「不安に思ってしまう」 is the Japanese speaker’s reaction when あいづち is absent.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 私はあなたの話を聞いていますよ
The passage says that あいづち is used to convey “I am listening to your story,” so option d directly matches the passage.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-q3.explanation: The pattern 「～ということを伝える」 means “to convey that…,” with 「～」 showing the message being conveyed. The main idea is that Japanese people often use あいづち to show that they are listening, while some other cultures may remain silent until the other person finishes speaking. The completed sentence is: だから、日本人と外国人では、「私はあなたの話を聞いていますよ」ということを伝える方法が違うことを理解して、コミュニケーションのやりかたを考えたほうがいい。 Translation: “Therefore, people should understand that Japanese people and foreigners use different ways to convey ‘I am listening to your story’ and think about how to communicate.” Option (a) is easy to confuse with the answer, but it lists specific あいづち expressions, whereas (d) states the meaning being conveyed.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 文化が違うことを理解して、よりよいコミュニケーションのやりかたを考えてみよう。
The passage says that we should understand cultural differences and think about better ways to communicate. Therefore, it does not say that あいづち must always be used or must never be used.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t13-q4.explanation: The pattern 文化が違うと means “when cultures are different,” while ～たほうがいい means “should” or “it is better to,” and is used to give advice. The main idea is that Japanese people and foreigners express “I am listening” differently, so they should adjust their communication method. The supporting sentence is: 「文化が違うと、コミュニケーションの方法も違う。だから、日本人と外国人では、「（　　　　）」ということを伝える方法が違うことを理解して、コミュニケーションのやりかたを考えたほうがいい。」, meaning: “When cultures are different, communication methods are also different; therefore, we should understand this and think about how to communicate.” To distinguish it from (d), remember that the passage does not completely reject あいづち; it concludes that communication can be comfortable whether people use it or not.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t14-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 前田さん
It is Thursday at 3 p.m., so 前田さん can be contacted because Thursday is one of the “other days,” and he prefers calls in the afternoon.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t14-q1.explanation: The pattern 「〜ので」 means “because…” and gives a reason; 「それ以外の日」 means “the other days,” while 「できれば午後がいいです」 expresses a preference for the afternoon. 前田さん’s notice means: “I do not think I can answer the phone on Monday, Tuesday, or Friday because I have classes and a part-time job; please call on the other days, preferably in the afternoon.” The relevant sentence is: 「月曜日、火曜日、金曜日は授業とアルバイトがあるので、電話に出られないと思います。それ以外の日に電話してください。できれば午後がいいです。」 A useful tip is to check both the day and the time: Thursday afternoon matches only 前田さん, not 中山さん or トムさん.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t14-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) B
Car B costs 7,000円, but the price is reduced by 2,000円 because Kim will pick it up in person, with the shop only a five-minute walk from school. The total is therefore exactly 5,000円, matching the budget.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t14-q2.explanation: In the question 「キムさんは5,000円ぐらいまでお金を払うつもりです。どの自転車をもらいますか。」 (Kim intends to pay up to about 5,000 yen; which bicycle will he receive?), the structure 『V-る + つもりです』 expresses the speaker’s intention, while 『まで』 marks the upper limit of the budget. The information for bicycle B states: 「値段は7,000円ですが、家まで取りに来てくれるなら、2,000円安くします。家は大学から歩いて5分くらいのところにあります。」 The conditional structure 『plain form + なら』, here 取りに来てくれるなら, gives the discount condition. Since the seller’s home is close to the university, Kim can pick it up himself and pay 5,000円. The main trap is choice C and the word 「ただ」 (free), but the additional costs must be included: about 5,000円 for repairs 「直すのに5,000円くらいかかる」 plus a 1,000-yen delivery fee 「1,000円お願いします」, bringing the actual total to 6,000円. Therefore, bicycle B is the only choice that fits Kim’s 5,000-yen budget.

default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t8-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) には
「には」 marks and emphasizes the place of existence, Kyoto; the sentence says that Kyoto has many old shrines and temples.
default.q.goukakumoshi3_n4-t8-q1.explanation: The pattern 「Nには Nがあります／います」 uses 「に」 to mark the place where something exists and 「は」 to state or emphasize the topic. This sentence means: “There are many old shrines and temples in Kyoto.” The original sentence is: 「京都には古い神社やお寺がたくさんあります。」 A useful distinction is that with あります／います, 「に」 is used for the place of existence, while 「で」 mainly marks the place where an action occurs.
